claims.text: Stainless steels are used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications.
Severe plastic deformation can produce ultrafine-grained stainless steel.
The ultrafine-grained state has a higher grain-boundary density than the coarse-grained baseline.
Grain boundaries in ultrafine-grained stainless steel act as fast diffusion channels for chromium toward the surface.
Faster chromium transport promotes chromium enrichment of the passive film.
High grain-boundary density enhances passive-film repair and rapid re-passivation after local disruption.
A chromium-rich passive film suppresses active metal dissolution and reduces the overall corrosion rate.
Ultrafine-grained stainless steel will have greater chromium enrichment in its passive film than coarse-grained stainless steel of the same composition.
Ultrafine-grained stainless steel will have a lower corrosion rate than the coarse-grained baseline.
XPS and electron-microscopy-based analysis can detect chromium enrichment in the passive film.
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy and potentiodynamic polarization can reveal the predicted corrosion-rate difference.
The proposed mechanism should hold under moderate chloride exposure and near-ambient to moderately elevated temperatures.
Extreme pH or temperature may compromise passive-film integrity regardless of microstructure.
Temperature can substantially affect chromium depletion or dissolution in duplex stainless steel.
Ni, Mo, or Cu may alter passive-film stability and repair kinetics in the steels under study.

Failure to observe both statistically significant passive-film chromium enrichment and a corresponding corrosion-rate decrease in the ultrafine-grained group would falsify the proposed governing mechanism.
